question: Does God have a body?
summary: Genesis shows Yahweh strolling through Eden 'in the cool of the day' — audible footsteps, physical movement. John 4:24 and Luke 24:39 then insist God is a spirit who by definition has no flesh and bones. Take your pick: a wandering-through-the-garden deity, or an incorporeal one.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read Genesis 3:8 as anthropomorphic theophany, not literal divine embodiment — the incorporeal God is described in bodily terms suited to human senses.

discrepancy.connective: Benjamin D. Sommer presses the strongest objection, arguing that several biblical texts — Genesis 3:8 among them, where God walks in the garden — really do conceive of Yahweh as having a body, against the later spiritualizing reading.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Genesis 3:8
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly, arguing that because God is an infinite Spirit with no bodily form, Genesis 3:8 describes His 'voice' and presence rather than a literal corporeal appearance — the harmonizing reading keyed to this verse.

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The voice is properly used here, for as God is an infinite Spirit, and cannot be confined to any form, so he can have no personal appearance.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes the two passages: Clarke grounds the Genesis 3:8 'voice/walking' in God's being an infinite Spirit with no bodily form — exactly the John 4:24 premise — so the Eden scene is not a corporeal deity. Single strongest reconcile; parity-capped to match the lone discrepancy pole.
excerpts.source_note_text: The voice of the Lord - The voice is properly used here, for as God is an infinite Spirit, and cannot be confined to any form, so he can have no personal appearance. It is very likely that God used to converse with them in the garden, and that the usual time was the decline of the day, לרוח היום leruach haiyom, in the evening breeze; and probably this was the time that our first parents employed in the more solemn acts of their religious worship, at which God was ever present. The time for this solemn worship is again come, and God is in his place; but Adam and Eve have sinned, and therefore, instead of being found in the place of worship, are hidden among the trees! Reader, how often has this been thy case!
